nameStory: Coulter's fleabane honors Thomas Coulter, an Irish botanist who explored the American West in the 1830s, collecting thousands of plant specimens. The "fleabane" part comes from an old belief that these daisy-like flowers could repel fleas when dried and scattered around homes. While we now know this probably didn't work very well, the name stuck to this whole group of wildflowers!
description: Coulter's fleabane is a western wildflower that looks like a classic daisy with bright white petals surrounding a golden center. This perennial herb grows 8-28 inches tall with an upright stem that may branch slightly or stay simple. It's native to moist mountain forests and meadows across the western United States, making any New England sighting quite remarkable. The plant typically produces one to four flower heads at the top of each stem, creating a cheerful display against its lance-shaped leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic daisy-like flower heads with bright golden yellow centers surrounded by up to 140 thin white petals (ray florets). Each flower head measures about half to three-quarters of an inch across and feels papery when touched.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long leaves that are somewhat lance-shaped to more rounded, growing both from the base and along the stem. Leaf edges may be smooth or have a few small teeth, and they feel slightly rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect perennial herb standing 8-28 inches tall with mostly unbranched stems. Plants often grow in small clusters and have a sturdy, upright appearance.

idTips.label: Flower Arrangement
idTips.description: Typically produces 1-4 flower heads clustered at the top of the stem, rather than many flowers scattered along branches. This creates a neat, organized appearance.

habitat: Given its extreme rarity in New England (only one recorded observation), Coulter's fleabane would most likely appear as an accidental introduction or garden escape. In its native western range, it prefers moist mountain forests and meadows at higher elevations. Any New England sighting would probably be in disturbed areas, along roadsides, or near areas where western wildflower seed mixes might have been planted.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with basal leaves forming rosettes. Stems begin elongating as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright white daisy-like flowers appearing from mid to late summer. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and produce small seeds with fluffy bristles. Leaves may begin to yellow as the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level as a perennial, with only roots surviving underground until spring growth resumes.

funFact: With only a single recorded observation in all of New England, spotting Coulter's fleabane here would be like finding botanical treasure - you'd be seeing a plant that's roughly 2,000 miles from home and probably traveled here accidentally in a seed mix or on someone's hiking boots!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other white-flowered fleabanes like daisy fleabane or annual fleabane, but Coulter's fleabane typically has fewer, larger flower heads (1-4 versus many) and more robust stems. The key difference is geographic - if you're seeing it in New England, double-check your identification since it's extremely rare here.
contextualKnowledge: The single New England observation of this western species highlights how plant databases track both native and non-native occurrences. Sometimes western wildflowers appear in eastern gardens through seed mixes labeled as "wildflower blends," leading to surprising sightings far from their natural range.
compareHints: Coulter's fleabane differs from common New England fleabanes by having fewer but larger flower heads and more robust growth. Unlike the weedy horseweed with its tiny, numerous flowers, or daisy fleabane with its many scattered blooms, Coulter's fleabane presents just 1-4 substantial flower heads per stem. It's also generally taller and more robust than the delicate robin's-plantain that blooms earlier in spring.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its showier cousins like daisy fleabane and annual fleabane, horseweed has extremely small, inconspicuous flowers that barely look like typical daisy-family blooms.
Among its fleabane relatives, robin's plantain stands out as the earliest bloomer with the most robust appearance and widest petals.
Among New England fleabanes, annual fleabane is distinguished by its relatively wide, obvious white petals and robust growth habit.
Daisy fleabane differs from its fleabane cousins by having the narrowest ray petals - they're almost thread-like compared to the broader petals of annual fleabane or Philadelphia fleabane.
Among New England's fleabanes, Philadelphia fleabane stands out with its extremely numerous thread-like petals (50-150) compared to daisy fleabane's fewer, broader petals (typically under 50).
Unlike the much more common daisy fleabane and annual fleabane which form branching clusters of many small flowers, hyssop-leaved fleabane usually produces just one flower head per stem.
